modules.title: Command line, files and Git
modules.targetGap: New to terminals, file paths, environments, packages and version control.

explanation.heading: Why this comes first
explanation.body: Every lab runs commands, edits files in folders, installs packages and records progress in Git. A little fluency here removes friction from all 30 units.

explanation.heading: The mental model
explanation.body: A terminal is a text conversation with your computer: you type a command, it runs, it prints a result. A path names where a file lives. Git records snapshots of your work so you can go back.

explanation.heading: The few commands you actually need
explanation.body: List, change directory, make a folder, run a script, and the core Git cycle: status, add, commit.
explanation.code:
pwd            # where am I
ls             # what is here (dir on Windows PowerShell: Get-ChildItem)
cd project     # go into a folder
python app.py  # run a script

git status
git add app.py
git commit -m "first working baseline"

exercises.prompt: You edited two files. Which command records a snapshot of just one of them?
exercises.answer: git add <that-file> then git commit -m "..." — staging selects what goes into the snapshot.

checkpoint.question: What is the difference between `git commit` and `git push`?
checkpoint.answer: commit records a snapshot in your local history; push sends committed snapshots to a remote like GitHub.

modules.evidencePrompt: Record the commands you ran and paste the output of `git log --oneline` for a small practice repo.

modules.title: Programming logic and Python
modules.targetGap: Little or no Python: values, control flow, functions, collections, errors, environments.

explanation.heading: Why this matters
explanation.body: Python is the language of every lab. You do not need to be an expert — you need to read, write and debug small programs confidently.

explanation.heading: Mental model
explanation.body: A program is data (values in variables and collections) plus decisions (if/else), repetition (loops) and reusable steps (functions). Errors are messages telling you exactly where a decision went wrong.

explanation.heading: Annotated example
explanation.body: A function that filters a list. Notice the parameter, the loop, the condition and the return.
explanation.code:
def open_tickets(tickets):
    result = []
    for t in tickets:          # repetition
        if t["status"] == "open":  # decision
            result.append(t)      # collect
    return result             # reusable output

print(open_tickets([{"status": "open"}, {"status": "closed"}]))
# -> [{'status': 'open'}]

explanation.heading: Isolated environments
explanation.body: Create a virtual environment per project so lab dependencies never collide.
explanation.code:
python -m venv .venv
# activate, then:
pip install numpy

exercises.prompt: Rewrite open_tickets using a list comprehension.
exercises.answer: [t for t in tickets if t["status"] == "open"]

checkpoint.question: What does a virtual environment give you?
checkpoint.answer: An isolated set of installed packages for one project, so versions don't clash with other projects or the system Python.

modules.evidencePrompt: Commit a small script with one function and a test, and note any error you fixed.

modules.title: Web foundations: HTTP, JSON and REST
modules.targetGap: Can program but doesn't understand browser/server flow, HTTP, JSON, status codes or CORS.

explanation.heading: Why this matters
explanation.body: You will call models and tools over HTTP APIs. Understanding the request/response cycle is the bridge from your code to a model.

explanation.heading: Mental model
explanation.body: A client sends a request (method + path + optional JSON body); a server routes it to a handler; the handler returns a response with a status code and usually JSON. 2xx = success, 4xx = your request was wrong, 5xx = the server failed.

explanation.heading: Worked walkthrough
explanation.body: A POST that creates a ticket and the response you'd expect.

explanation.heading: The same-origin boundary (CORS)
explanation.body: Browsers block a page on one origin from calling another origin unless the server opts in with CORS headers. This is a frequent early confusion when a fetch 'mysteriously' fails.

exercises.prompt: A request returns 401. What category of problem is it, and whose?
exercises.answer: A 4xx client error — specifically missing/invalid authentication. The request must supply valid credentials.

checkpoint.question: What does a 500 status code tell you versus a 400?
checkpoint.answer: 500 means the server failed while handling a valid-looking request; 400 means the request itself was malformed. They point you at different code.

modules.evidencePrompt: Call any public JSON API with an HTTP client and record the method, status code and a field from the JSON.

modules.title: Frontend foundations
modules.targetGap: Needs enough HTML/CSS/JS/TS, components, state and accessibility to understand and extend the portal.

explanation.heading: Why this matters
explanation.body: The learning portal is a React app. Understanding components and state helps you read it and later build a simple client for your agent.

explanation.heading: Mental model
explanation.body: A component is a function that returns UI from its inputs (props) and its changeable data (state). When state changes, the view re-renders. This idea returns later as LangGraph state.

explanation.heading: Annotated example
explanation.body: A counter: state plus an event handler.

explanation.heading: Accessibility is not optional
explanation.body: Controls need labels, keyboard operation, visible focus and sufficient contrast — the same standard this portal holds itself to.

exercises.prompt: Why must an icon-only button still have accessible text?
exercises.answer: Screen-reader users and keyboard users need a name to know what the control does; use aria-label or visually-hidden text.

checkpoint.question: What triggers a re-render in a component-based UI?
checkpoint.answer: A change to the component's state (or props); the framework recomputes and updates the view.

modules.evidencePrompt: Build a tiny component with one piece of state and note how you made a control keyboard-accessible.

modules.title: Backend and data foundations
modules.targetGap: Needs Flask/FastAPI concepts, SQL/data modeling, object storage, caching and observability basics.

explanation.heading: Why this matters
explanation.body: RAG and agents are backends: they route requests, query data stores, cache results and emit logs. Your backend instincts transfer directly.

explanation.heading: Connect it to what you know
explanation.body: A Flask/FastAPI route that reads a row by id is the same shape as a retrieval endpoint that reads a chunk by id. A database index that speeds lookups is the ancestor of a vector index.

explanation.heading: Annotated example
explanation.body: A typed FastAPI route returning JSON.

explanation.heading: Data modeling and filtering
explanation.body: A WHERE clause filters rows; later you'll combine metadata filters with vector similarity. Observability (logs/metrics) tells you what actually happened in production.

exercises.prompt: How is a database index like a vector index?
exercises.answer: Both trade extra structure/space to make lookups fast — exact-match/range for a DB index, approximate nearest-neighbor for a vector index.

checkpoint.question: Why return 404 instead of an empty 200 when a ticket is missing?
checkpoint.answer: The status code communicates the outcome precisely so clients can react correctly; an empty 200 hides the real state.

modules.evidencePrompt: Sketch a two-table schema for the support system and write one SQL query with a WHERE clause.

modules.title: Math and data foundations
modules.targetGap: Needs algebra, vectors, matrices, probability, derivatives/gradients, NumPy and pandas.

explanation.heading: Why this matters
explanation.body: Weights, embeddings, attention and training are all built from vectors, matrices and gradients. A little comfort here removes the mystery from the deep-learning units.

explanation.heading: Mental model
explanation.body: A vector is an ordered list of numbers; a matrix is a table; a dot product multiplies matching entries and sums them. A derivative is 'how much the output changes if I nudge the input'; a gradient collects those nudges for many parameters.

explanation.heading: Annotated example
explanation.body: A weighted sum in NumPy — the core of a neuron.
explanation.code:
import numpy as np
features = np.array([3, 5, 1])
weights  = np.array([0.4, -0.2, 0.9])
output = features @ weights + 0.5   # dot product + bias
print(output)  # 2.6

exercises.prompt: Compute the dot product of [1,0,2] and [3,4,1] by hand.

checkpoint.question: In plain words, what does a gradient tell you during training?
checkpoint.answer: Which direction and how much to change each weight to reduce the loss a little.

modules.evidencePrompt: Reproduce the weighted-sum example in NumPy and change one weight; record how the output changes.

modules.title: Delivery foundations: Docker, cloud, CI/CD
modules.targetGap: Needs Docker, cloud responsibility mapping, CI/CD, IAM and reliability/cost awareness.

explanation.heading: Why this matters
explanation.body: The capstone deploys a real service. Containers make labs reproducible, and the shared-responsibility model clarifies what you own versus the cloud.

explanation.heading: Mental model
explanation.body: A container packages your app plus its dependencies so it runs the same everywhere. In a managed/serverless cloud, the provider patches the infrastructure while you own your code, config, data and access (IAM).

explanation.heading: Connect it to agents
explanation.body: IAM permissions for a cloud resource are the same idea as least-privilege tool permissions for an agent: grant only what is needed.

exercises.prompt: In managed serverless, who patches the OS?
exercises.answer: The cloud provider, under the shared-responsibility model; you still own app config, data and access control.

checkpoint.question: Why does a container make a lab more reproducible?
checkpoint.answer: It bundles the exact runtime and dependencies, so 'works on my machine' becomes 'works the same everywhere'.

modules.evidencePrompt: Write a minimal Dockerfile for a Python script and note the base image and why you chose it.
